meta.descriptionEn: In November 2013, one of the most intense tropical cyclones ever recorded tore across the central Philippines. Typhoon Haiyan, known locally as Yolanda, arrived with some of the strongest winds ever estimated, but the greatest danger came from the sea itself. A rising wall of water swept into Tacloban and the Visayas, leaving cities flattened and communications gone. Why did a storm that was so closely tracked still catch so many people unprepared? What do warning signals really tell us, and what do they leave out? This documentary follows Haiyan from a broad low-pressure area near Micronesia to its devastating landfall, the struggle for relief, and the changes that followed.
meta.descriptionUr: November 2013 mein Typhoon Haiyan, jise Philippines mein Yolanda kaha gaya, tarikh ke sab se shadeed toofanon mein se ek ban kar Philippines se takraya. Is ki hawaon ka andaza record satah ka tha, lekin asal khatra samundar ka paani tha. Tacloban aur Visayas mein storm surge ne shehar tabah kar diye. Sawal yeh hai ke itne qareeb se nigrani ke bawajood log kyun tayyar nahin the? Is documentary mein dekhein Haiyan ki poori kahani aur is ke baad aane wali tabdeeliyan.

articleEn: On the morning of 8 November 2013, the full force of Typhoon Haiyan struck the Philippine city of Tacloban. Yet the greatest damage seems to have come less from the wind than from the water. A storm surge 5.2 meters high rose over the terminal building at Tacloban airport. The water reached the height of the second floor, and the building was destroyed.

The city's Convention Center was an evacuation shelter. Its entire ground floor was flooded, and many people had no chance to get to safety. Sebastian Rhodes Stampa, head of the UN disaster assessment team, said the destruction was on a very large scale. He compared the scene to the devastation seen after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. Debris lay across the roads and vehicles were scattered about. There were no phone signals, and many towns were cut off from the rest of the world. It took the world several days to understand the whole picture.

But the real question is this: how did a storm that had been tracked for several days bring such enormous destruction? Were there gaps in the warnings? And did the most important message actually reach people? In this story we follow the typhoon from its birth to the devastation, and also look at what changed afterwards.

articleEn: The story begins on 2 November 2013, when the JTWC started watching a broad low-pressure area near Pohnpei. It lay about 425 kilometers east-southeast of Pohnpei, an island in the Federated States of Micronesia. At that point it was just a system, but conditions around it were favorable. On 3 November the JMA classified it as a tropical depression, and the next day it became a tropical storm. At 00:00 UTC on 4 November it was given a name: Haiyan, the 30th named storm of the 2013 Pacific typhoon season. A day earlier, when the JTWC announced Tropical Depression 31W, tropical storm warnings had already been issued for Chuuk Lagoon, Losap and Poluwat. The storm was moving west along the southern edge of a subtropical ridge.

By 5 November rapid intensification had begun. Satellite images showed a dense cloud center with an eye forming inside it, and that day Haiyan became a full typhoon. On 6 November PAGASA gave it a new name in the Philippines: Yolanda, as the storm approached the Philippine Area of Responsibility. The same day, at about 12:00 UTC, the JTWC estimated that Haiyan had become a super typhoon, equivalent to Category 5 on the Saffir-Simpson scale. It was now heading toward Palau. Typhoon warnings had been issued for Yap State and Palau on 5 November.

Kayangel, an island in Palau, lay closest to the storm's path. The government ordered people to evacuate, but most ignored the order and stayed. Haiyan's eye then passed directly over the island. The storm surge flooded all of Kayangel and the winds brought down trees, and every house on the island was destroyed. Remarkably, no deaths or serious injuries were reported. However, 69 people were left homeless, and relief supplies were delivered by helicopter.

Damage was lighter on other Micronesian islands. In Eauripik, for example, a canoe house and three homes were damaged, and banana and breadfruit trees were affected. In four days, then, a system that began as a broad low-pressure area near Pohnpei had become a super typhoon equivalent to Category 5. Its next target was the Philippines. But before it got there, Haiyan's strength had to be measured, and that is where a tangled story begins.

articleEn: Now let's talk numbers. How fast were Haiyan's winds? Surprisingly, the question has more than one answer. At 12:00 UTC on 7 November, the JMA put its ten-minute sustained winds at a peak of 230 km/h, with a minimum central pressure of 895 hPa. Six hours later the JTWC estimated one-minute sustained winds at 315 km/h, with gusts up to 380 km/h. These are two very different numbers for the same storm.

Other agencies gave their own figures. PAGASA estimated ten-minute sustained winds of 235 km/h and gusts of 275 km/h at landfall in Guiuan. The Hong Kong Observatory reported ten-minute winds of 285 km/h before landfall. The China Meteorological Administration reported two-minute sustained winds of about 78 m/s, or 280 km/h. So where does the difference come from? One reason is that agencies average wind speed over different periods: one minute, two minutes or ten minutes. That means 230 and 315 cannot be compared directly. All the numbers describe the same extremely powerful storm, measured on different scales. Based on the JTWC's one-minute estimate, Haiyan is counted among the most powerful tropical cyclones ever observed.

At 20:40 UTC on 7 November, Haiyan's eye made its first landfall in the Philippines at Guiuan, Eastern Samar, with the storm at full strength. According to the JTWC, one-minute winds were then 305 km/h. On that scale it was the strongest recorded storm ever to make landfall, a record later broken by Typhoon Goni in 2020. Still, in 2013 Haiyan was the most intense and deadliest tropical cyclone in the world.

The storm's structure was also unusual. It showed some characteristics of an annular tropical cyclone, though a strong convective band remained to the west. It then crossed the Visayas region of the Philippines and made five more landfalls on the way, including Tolosa, Leyte.

Yet something matters more than these numbers. The wind was very strong, but the main cause of damage and loss of life appears to have been the storm surge. In Tacloban the surge reached 5.2 meters. When the debate was about wind speed, how much attention went to the wall of water? That question leads us onward. First we will see how a storm builds a wall of water, and then what the warnings said.

articleEn: What exactly is storm surge? It is the rise of seawater above the normal tide level, and it does not include waves. The biggest cause is strong wind. When wind pushes water toward the coast over a long distance, the water level at the shore begins to rise. This is called wind setup. Wind also creates surface currents, and the effect grows with water depth.

The second factor is air pressure. When pressure at the storm's center is low, the sea surface rises, by roughly 10 mm for every hPa of drop. For example, in a large storm with a 100 hPa drop, pressure alone could raise the water by about 1 meter. Then there is the effect of the Earth's rotation. The Coriolis effect turns currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, and a turn toward the coast can increase the surge. Waves are a separate matter, but near the shore they also bring a lot of water forward. A wave climbing a slope can reach up to twice its own height.

Next, consider the depth of the sea. Where the shelf is narrow and deep water lies close to shore, the surge is smaller but the waves are stronger. By contrast, on a wide, shallow shelf the surge has less room to spread, so the wind pushes it toward the coast. The height of the land matters too. Areas only a few meters above the sea face a greater risk of surge water pushing far inland. The size of the storm also makes a difference. If the diameter doubles, the perimeter doubles but the area grows four times, and the surge has less room to spread. In Haiyan's case, reports say Tacloban's coastal population was hit hardest because the city lies between Samar and Leyte.

How is such a surge forecast? America's National Hurricane Center uses a model called SLOSH. It takes in central pressure, storm size, speed, track and maximum wind speed. The model's accuracy is stated to be within 20 percent. Historically, surges have been extremely deadly. In the 1970 Bhola cyclone up to 500,000 people died, and in 2008 Cyclone Nargis killed more than 138,000 in Myanmar. The second deadliest surge of this century was Typhoon Haiyan's. More than 6,000 people died, and damage was estimated at 14 billion dollars. So the question remains: in what form did the warning about storm surge reach people?

articleEn: The story of the warnings starts on 3 November. The JTWC classified Tropical Depression 31W, and tropical storm warnings were issued for Chuuk Lagoon, Losap and Poluwat. Then on 6 November, as the storm neared the Philippine Area of Responsibility, PAGASA issued Signal No. 1 for much of the Visayas and Mindanao. This was the lowest of four levels. As the storm came closer, warnings spread to Luzon and grew more severe in eastern areas. By the evening of 7 November, Signal No. 4, the highest level, was raised for Biliran, Eastern Samar, Leyte, Northern Cebu, Metro Cebu, Samar and Southern Leyte. This level meant winds above 185 km/h were expected.

Note that the whole system is built around wind speed. PAGASA's system at the time ran on wind speed, with a stated lead time of 36 hours for Signal 1 and 12 hours for Signal 4. The storm was moving very fast. PAGASA issued warnings of various levels for about 60 of the country's 80 provinces, including Metro Manila.

Preparations were made as well. Classes were canceled in Samar and Leyte, and residents of areas at risk of flood or landslide were ordered to evacuate. Police were deployed in the Bicol Region, and President Noynoy Aquino, who was in office at the time, told the military to send planes and helicopters to the expected affected area. But there was a complication. Some areas were already affected by the Bohol earthquake: a magnitude 7.2 quake had struck Cebu and Bohol two weeks earlier.

Now back to Palau. A mandatory evacuation order was issued for Kayangel, but most residents ignored it and the storm passed right over them. No one died in Kayangel, although the whole island was flooded and every house was destroyed. 69 people were left homeless.

In Vietnam, preparations at the highest level were activated on 8 November. About 600,000 people were evacuated from southern and central provinces and 200,000 from northern provinces. Alerts went out to 85,328 vessels to head for safe water. About 460,000 soldiers and other officials were mobilized to help with evacuation. The UN's Pratibha Mehta credited the Vietnamese government's measures with saving many lives. Yet many residents complained that the warnings came late.

So where was the gap? On one side were evacuation orders; on the other, a storm among the most powerful in history. And then, at 4:40 on the morning of 8 November, the eye of the storm struck Philippine land. Its first stop was Guiuan.

articleEn: At 4:40 a.m. on 8 November, which was 20:40 UTC on 7 November, Haiyan's eye struck Guiuan, Eastern Samar, at the peak of its intensity. Guiuan is a fishing town. Almost every building suffered at least some damage, and many were flattened completely. Mayor Christopher Gonzalez deserves to be remembered here. He appealed to people again and again to evacuate, and he called the storm a deluge. Of the town's 45,000 residents, 87 died, 931 were injured and 23 were declared missing. Every number is a family's grief. U.S. Navy medical officer Captain Russell Hays estimated that without the Mayor's efforts, as many as 4,500 people could have died in Guiuan alone.

Then silence fell. For several days there was no contact with Guiuan, and the extent of the damage became clear only when Philippine Air Force personnel arrived on 10 November. Meanwhile a local priest rode a motorcycle from Guiuan to Catbalogan and Calbayog, carrying photographs of the destruction on his mobile phone. On the morning of 8 November the media had been broadcasting live, but before noon all communications in the Visayas went down. Even the president's communications department had difficulty reaching Mar Roxas and Voltaire Gazmin in Tacloban.

Now to Tacloban. The city lies between Samar and Leyte, and its coastal areas, especially San Jose, were hit hardest. The airport terminal was wrecked by a 5.2-meter surge that reached the height of the second floor. A surge of 4 meters near the airport was also estimated. In Tacloban's eastern coastal areas, some parts were washed away completely. Flooding reached about 1 km inland on the eastern coast. According to Tecson John Lim, about 90 percent of the city had been destroyed. UN team head Sebastian Rhodes Stampa called it destruction on a massive scale.

Tacloban's Convention Center was an evacuation shelter. Its entire ground floor was submerged in the surge, and the fast-rising water caught many people by surprise. The place that had become a refuge was itself caught in the water, which is still a sobering thought. On Calicoan Island in Eastern Samar, the storm lifted and hurled car-sized boulders, the heaviest weighing 180 tons. Some boulders traveled about 10 meters upward. This is considered the heaviest weight moved by a tropical cyclone in record-keeping.

According to reports, the wind was fierce, but the main cause of damage and loss of life was the surge. The worst destruction was concentrated on the eastern coast of Samar and Leyte. And as aid began reaching Tacloban and the surrounding areas, a new question arose: was it arriving fast enough?

articleEn: Before noon on 8 November, all communications in the Visayas had collapsed. Until morning the media had been showing the destruction live, and then suddenly everything went quiet. The president's communications office had trouble reaching Interior Secretary Mar Roxas and Defense Secretary Voltaire Gazmin, who were in Tacloban. Major roads were blocked by fallen trees. 453 domestic and international flights were canceled, and several airports stayed closed on 8 and 9 November.

The real problem was logistics. Aid reached local airports, but because the roads were blocked, most of the supplies stayed there. According to estimates on 13 November, only about 20 percent of the affected population of Tacloban was receiving aid. Access to clean water was also very limited. Thousands of people wanted to leave the city on C-130 cargo planes. With no electricity, planes could operate only in daylight. On the morning of 12 November, thousands broke through barriers toward the aircraft, but police and troops pushed them back. Later that day, as a U.S. cargo plane was landing, the scene repeated.

On 14 November a BBC correspondent called Tacloban a war zone. Amid hunger and despair, looting began in the city. Two malls and several grocery stores were targeted, and food was even snatched from some relief trucks. City administrator Tecson John Lim said it was not criminality but self-preservation. Interior Secretary Roxas rejected claims of anarchy. Keeping order was difficult because only 100 of Tacloban's 1,300 police officers could report for duty. Checkpoints were set up and a curfew was imposed. As the presence of government law enforcement grew, conditions slowly stabilized. President Aquino had also considered imposing martial law.

Now the biggest question: how many people died? By 17 April 2016 the NDRRMC had confirmed 6,300 deaths, 5,902 of them in Eastern Visayas. But the true number is still unclear. Government sources put it at 4,000 to 6,000, while some sources claim up to 15,000. Three days after the storm, President Aquino gave his own estimate of 2,000 to 5,000 and rejected the 10,000 estimate. The argument over numbers became a dispute of its own.

The scale of the damage was also huge: 28,688 injured, 550,928 homes totally destroyed and 589,404 partially damaged. By one estimate 1.8 million people were left homeless. The government was criticized for a lack of coordination between preparations and institutions. Five days later many survivors were still struggling for food, water and shelter. The government's answer was that the response was slow because the local system in the affected areas had itself collapsed, and many local officials had been victims of the storm. According to Roxas, the scale of the relief operation was overwhelming. So what did the world do? And how much damage did the storm do in other countries?

articleEn: When news of the destruction got out, international help began to move. The United Nations announced it would expand relief operations, but damaged infrastructure was a major obstacle. The UN activated the Cluster System, in which UN and non-UN humanitarian organizations work together to restore health, shelter, nutrition and livelihoods. The World Health Organization led the largest of these, the Health Cluster. It prepared guidance on donations so that suitable medicines and supplies would reach this emergency.

The United States gave 51.9 million dollars in aid under Operation Damayan and deployed Marines, Navy and Air Force personnel for humanitarian work. China's initial aid was debated. Its government and the Chinese Red Cross each gave 100,000 dollars in cash. Later China gave a further 1.64 million dollars and sent its naval hospital ship Peace Ark for relief. Reaction inside China was mixed. Among NGOs, Taiwan's Tzu Chi Foundation ran a cash-for-work program in Tacloban from 20 November to 8 December, with up to 31,000 people taking part daily. The work cleared the city's debris and supported the local economy. Tzu Chi also gave emergency cash aid to more than 60,000 families.

Now to other countries. In Taiwan, 8-meter waves on the coast at Gongliao swept away 16 people, of whom 8 died. In southern China 30 people died and an estimated 1.21 million were affected. Direct economic loss was 4.58 billion yuan, or 752 million dollars. In Vietnam, Haiyan killed 18 people and injured 93, with economic losses of 669 billion dong, or 31.67 million dollars. In the Philippines, losses were estimated at 95.48 billion pesos, or 2.2 billion dollars. Another source, however, mentions 14 billion dollars. The sources differ here.

This was not the city's first great disaster. Tacloban had been struck by devastating typhoons in 1897 and 1912. The November 1912 typhoon nearly destroyed Tacloban. Deaths in Tacloban and Capiz were 15,000, equal at the time to half the population of those cities. So the region had faced such storms before. Had anything been learned from past experience? And finally, what changed after this disaster, and which questions still demand answers?

articleEn: After the storm came a symbolic change of names. In 2014 the Typhoon Committee retired the name Haiyan and replaced it with Bailu, which was first used in the 2019 season. PAGASA also removed the name Yolanda and chose Yasmin in its place, which was not used in 2017. At the time of Haiyan, PAGASA's signals were based on wind speed. In 2013 there were four levels, whereas today's wind signals have five. In 2017 the US National Hurricane Center introduced a new system of storm surge watches and warnings for the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. Many methods are used around the world to protect against storm surge: flood barriers, coastal dunes, mangroves, better construction, early warning, education and evacuation plans. The Philippines also planned to replant mangroves in coastal areas and protect the surviving ones, which is part of soft adaptation.

Housing, however, has remained a long-running problem. By September 2021, about 148,000 of the 204,000 planned housing units for Haiyan survivors had been completed. Some survivors protested delays and backlogs. In 2018 NEDA confirmed that the 2016 Yolanda Recovery program budget had not been used by 31 December 2017.

Was the storm linked to climate change? The 2013 UN Climate Change Conference was under way at the time, and Yeb Saño announced a fast there. Will Steffen said that storms draw energy from ocean heat and that sea-surface temperatures are rising worldwide. Myles Allen said that, by the current consensus, climate change is not increasing the risk of hurricanes, but there are physical arguments for a risk of more intense storms. The Huffington Post wrote that, according to the Forest Management Bureau, 70 percent of the Philippines' forests have been cut since 1900, which raises the chance of dangerous flooding.

The storm also changed thinking about mental health. It was called a trauma milestone for mental health awareness in the Philippines, where counseling had once been seen as weakness. Finally, MV Eva Jocelyn, the cargo ship the storm pushed onto land, is today a memorial park in Tacloban in memory of Yolanda.

The biggest question is still open: what was the real death toll? The official figure is 6,300, but estimates ranged from 2,000 to 15,000, and many people are still missing today. Another question remains: when the next such storm comes, will people understand the danger of the surge in advance? shorts.titleEn: The Water That Reached the Second Floor in Tacloban
shorts.text: ایک airport کی terminal building پر 5.2 meter اونچا پانی چڑھ آیا! 8 November 2013 کو Tacloban پر Typhoon Haiyan ٹوٹ پڑا۔ مگر سب سے بڑا نقصان ہوا سے زیادہ پانی نے کیا۔ Storm surge اتنی اونچی تھی کہ پانی دوسری منزل تک پہنچ گیا۔ شہر کا Convention Center ایک evacuation shelter تھا۔ اس کی پوری پہلی منزل پانی میں ڈوب گئی، اور بہت سے لوگوں کو سنبھلنے کا موقع نہ ملا۔ UN کی disaster assessment team کے سربراہ Sebastian Rhodes Stampa نے اسے 2004 کے Indian Ocean tsunami کے بعد دیکھی گئی تباہی جیسا بتایا۔ سوال یہ ہے کہ یہ پانی آخر کیسے بنتا ہے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek airport ki terminal building par 5.2 meter oonchा paani chadh aaya! 8 November 2013 ko Tacloban par Typhoon Haiyan toot para. Magar sab se bara nuqsan hawa se zyada paani ne kiya. Storm surge itni oonchi thi ke paani doosri manzil tak pahunch gaya. Shehar ka Convention Center ek evacuation shelter tha. Is ki poori pehli manzil paani mein doob gayi, aur bohat se logon ko sambhalne ka mauqa na mila. UN ki disaster assessment team ke sarbarah Sebastian Rhodes Stampa ne ise 2004 ke Indian Ocean tsunami ke baad dekhi gayi tabahi jaisa bataya. Sawal yeh hai ke yeh paani aakhir kaise banta hai? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 8 November 2013, Typhoon Haiyan's storm surge reached the second floor of Tacloban airport's terminal.
A UN team leader compared the scale of destruction to the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami.

shorts.titleEn: One Typhoon, Many Wind Speeds: Haiyan's Numbers
shorts.text: ایک ہی طوفان، اور ہوا کی رفتار کے کئی مختلف numbers! یہ کیسے ممکن ہے؟ 7 November 2013 کو 12:00 UTC پر JMA نے Haiyan کی ten-minute sustained winds 230 km/h بتائیں۔ Central pressure 895 hPa تھا۔ چھ گھنٹے بعد JTWC نے one-minute sustained winds کا اندازہ 315 km/h لگایا، اور gusts 380 km/h تک۔ Philippines کی agency PAGASA نے Guiuan میں landfall کے وقت ten-minute winds 235 km/h اور gusts 275 km/h بتائیں۔ Hong Kong Observatory نے landfall سے پہلے ten-minute winds 285 km/h کہا۔ یعنی ایک منٹ اور دس منٹ کی اوسط والے numbers ساتھ ساتھ موجود ہیں۔ تو آخر Haiyan کتنا طاقتور تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek hi toofan, aur hawa ki raftar ke kai mukhtalif numbers! Yeh kaise mumkin hai? 7 November 2013 ko 12:00 UTC par JMA ne Haiyan ki ten-minute sustained winds 230 km/h batayin. Central pressure 895 hPa tha. Chhe ghante baad JTWC ne one-minute sustained winds ka andaza 315 km/h lagaya, aur gusts 380 km/h tak. Philippines ki agency PAGASA ne Guiuan mein landfall ke waqt ten-minute winds 235 km/h aur gusts 275 km/h batayin. Hong Kong Observatory ne landfall se pehle ten-minute winds 285 km/h kaha. Yani ek minute aur das minute ki ausat wale numbers saath saath maujood hain. To aakhir Haiyan kitna taqatwar tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Different agencies reported different wind speeds for Typhoon Haiyan, from 230 km/h to 315 km/h.
We look at why the numbers differ, including the different averaging periods used.

shorts.titleEn: The Mayor Who Urged Everyone to Evacuate Before Haiyan
shorts.text: ایک mayor کی اپیل نے ہزاروں زندگیاں کیسے بچائیں؟ 8 November 2013 کی صبح 4:40 بجے Haiyan کی آنکھ Guiuan سے ٹکرائی۔ یہ Eastern Samar کا ایک fishing town ہے۔ تقریباً ہر عمارت کو کم از کم جزوی نقصان پہنچا۔ مگر Mayor Christopher Gonzalez نے لوگوں سے بار بار evacuate ہونے کی اپیل کی تھی۔ انہوں نے طوفان کو delubyo کہا۔ قصبے کی 45,000 آبادی میں سے 87 لوگ جان سے گئے اور 23 لاپتہ قرار دیے گئے۔ U.S. Navy کے Captain Russell Hays کا اندازہ تھا کہ Mayor کی کوششوں کے بغیر صرف Guiuan میں 4,500 تک لوگوں کی جان جا سکتی تھی۔ پھر Guiuan کے بعد Haiyan کہاں گیا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek mayor ki appeal ne hazaron zindagiyan kaise bachayin? 8 November 2013 ki subah 4:40 baje Haiyan ki aankh Guiuan se takrai. Yeh Eastern Samar ka ek fishing town hai. Taqriban har imarat ko kam az kam juzvi nuqsan pohncha. Magar Mayor Christopher Gonzalez ne logon se bar bar evacuate hone ki appeal ki thi. Unhon ne toofan ko delubyo kaha. Qasbe ki 45,000 abadi mein se 87 log jaan se gaye aur 23 lapata qarar diye gaye. U.S. Navy ke Captain Russell Hays ka andaza tha ke Mayor ki koshishon ke baghair sirf Guiuan mein 4,500 tak logon ki jaan ja sakti thi. Phir Guiuan ke baad Haiyan kahan gaya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Typhoon Haiyan first hit Guiuan, Eastern Samar, where Mayor Christopher Gonzalez had repeatedly urged residents to evacuate.
A US Navy officer estimated his efforts saved many lives.
